name: 25503-1k1k-qwen3next80b-4gpu
hardware: 4x H100 80GB HBM3 -- four GPUs of one a3 node, one node, NVLink within the node.
parallelism: TP=4, EP on, PP=1, DP=1, one vLLM engine -- 'TEP4'. Four-way tensor parallel is what holds 162.7 GB of weights on 80 GB cards; expert parallelism places whole experts on each of the four ranks instead of slicing every expert across all four. Both are part of the question: this setup is about what a 512-expert layer costs when the experts are distributed.
architecture: hybrid sparse mixture-of-experts decoder in bfloat16 -- 48 layers, hidden size 2048, 512 experts with 10 active per token, expert intermediate size 512 plus a shared expert of 512, silu-gated, every layer sparse. Attention is interleaved: every 4th layer is full attention (16 heads over 2 KV heads at head_dim 256, partial rotary 0.25), the other 36 are gated-DeltaNet linear-attention layers with a 4-wide causal convolution, so only 12 of 48 layers keep a KV cache and the rest keep a fixed-size recurrent state per sequence. 262144-token native window. 41 safetensors shards, 162.7 GB of bf16 weights, ~81 B parameters total and ~3 B active per token. UNQUANTIZED IS THE DECLARED SETUP, not an oversight: the checkpoint is served at full bf16 precision and no quantization is applied.
load_profile: concurrent (closed loop), streams=256, warmup 10%, cooldown 10%, bounded at 1024 requests with a 1800 s safety cap. 256 is CHOSEN and is deep in the throughput regime, where every stream is decoding almost all of the time. 1024 requests is CHOSEN: four full rounds of 256, leaving ~819 measured requests after warmup and cooldown, which is roughly two to three minutes of traffic. Warmup and cooldown at 10% are CHOSEN and matter here because the first requests pay CUDA-graph capture, weight-layout work and any first-call kernel setup. Seed static 25503, CHOSEN -- pinning the item number keeps the synthetic corpus reproducible per item.
workload: synthetic `synthetic_text`, single turn: 1024 prompt tokens and 1024 output tokens per request, min == max == the mean on both, temperature 0, sent as plain text completions rather than through a chat template. TWO HUNDRED AND FIFTY-SIX STREAMS OF 1024-IN / 1024-OUT IS A DECODE-DOMINATED MIXTURE: each stream pays one 1024-token prefill and then a thousand single-token steps, so with 256 in flight the engine is almost always running a large decode batch with the occasional prefill folded into the same step by chunked prefill. That is what makes every layer's 512-expert routed matmul the recurring work of the run. The scheduler's 8192-token step budget admits at most eight of those prefills per step. Requests run to the full 1024 output tokens: `ignore_eos` is set whenever the scenario declares an output length, so no request stops early. WIRE LENGTH EQUALS DECLARED LENGTH HERE, EXACTLY -- and that is a property of `request_format: plain`, not a general one. The generator encodes sampled text, truncates the id list to 1024 and decodes that slice back; the plain format then sends the result as a raw completion with no chat template, no role prefixes and no generation prompt, so the round trip is lossless. MEASURED on this checkpoint's own tokenizer: 20 seeds out of 20 give exactly 1024. Under a chat template the same workload would run some percent long, but none is applied here, so a reported prompt count that is NOT 1024 is real drift and must be investigated rather than excused. Temperature 0 and the plain completions format are CHOSEN: greedy plain text is the least elaborate thing that produces the declared shape.
purpose: A long-context text completion service on an 80-billion-parameter sparse model, serving 256 concurrent 1k-in, 1k-out requests across four GPUs.
launch:
# A hybrid sparse mixture-of-experts decoder in bf16: 48 layers, hidden 2048, 512 experts with
# 10 active per token, expert intermediate 512 plus a shared expert of 512, silu-gated.
model: Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct

# BOTH LINES ARE THE SETUP, not decoration. Four-way tensor parallel is what holds 162.7 GB of
# weights on 80 GB cards, and expert parallelism is how the 512 experts are placed: with it on,
# the experts of each MoE layer are split across the four ranks and each rank owns whole experts,
# instead of every rank holding a slice of every expert. Data parallelism is left at 1, so this
# is TEP4: one engine, four ranks, tensor parallel for the dense parts and expert parallel for
# the sparse ones.
tensor-parallel-size: 4
enable-expert-parallel: true

# The scheduler's per-step token budget, and the operating point is a statement about it: with
# 1024-token prompts, at most eight prefills fit in one step alongside whatever is decoding.
max-num-batched-tokens: 8192

# PINNED, AND LOAD-BEARING. Do not delete this as "the default". The engine is built through
# AsyncLLMEngine.from_engine_args, whose usage context is UsageContext.ENGINE_CONTEXT. That key
# is in NEITHER per-context table of `_set_default_args` (arg_utils.py at this commit: LLM_CLASS
# 1024 / OPENAI_API_SERVER 1024 sequences on a >=70 GiB non-A100 card), so it falls through to
# the library default in config/scheduler.py -- 128 -- which is HALF the concurrency this item
# declares and would silently turn a 256-stream closed loop into a 128-deep queue. 1024 is what a
# real `vllm serve` resolves to on this card at this commit. `max-num-batched-tokens` is stated
# above and so never reaches that table.
max-num-seqs: 1024

# V1 would otherwise default it on. It buys nothing here -- every prompt is 1024 freshly sampled
# tokens, so no request can hit another's blocks -- and turning it off removes the hashing work
# and one source of run-to-run variation.
enable-prefix-caching: false

# The scheduler prepares the next step while the current one is still on the GPU. Note it forces
# the multiprocessing executor backend (arg_utils.py at this commit), which is what a 4-way
# tensor-parallel engine uses anyway.
async-scheduling: true

# Written out because the operating point is a statement about it: V1 forces chunked prefill on
# for a generation model at this commit, so a 1024-token prompt is scheduled into the same steps
# as running decodes.
enable-chunked-prefill: true

# CHOSEN. With no window set the engine would take the checkpoint's full 262144. The workload's
# worst case is 1024 prompt + 1024 output = 2048 tokens; 4096 is the plainest value that clears
# it and keeps the KV pool and the per-sequence state fixed.
max-model-len: 4096

# CHOSEN. 0.90 is vLLM's own default here, written out so a change of default cannot move the
# memory budget. 0.90 x 80 GB - ~38 GiB of weights leaves ~34 GiB per card for KV and recurrent
# state, against a resident worst case of 256 x 2048 tokens -- and only 12 of the 48 layers keep
# a KV cache at all. Memory is not the binding resource here.
gpu-memory-utilization: 0.90

# --- DELIBERATELY ABSENT:
#   dtype                  -- the checkpoint declares bfloat16; letting the engine read it is
#                             what this setup wants.
#   quantization           -- none. This checkpoint is not quantized, and that is the point of
#                             the setup: it is served at full bf16 precision.
#   data-parallel-size     -- 1, the default.
#   enforce-eager          -- NOT set. The engine's own CUDA-graph defaults for decode are the
#                             operating point of interest.
#   block-size, scheduling-policy, seed, kv-cache-dtype, mamba-cache-dtype -- left at the
#                             engine's defaults.
#   --host / --port        -- server-side only; the engine runs in-process here.
